chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
title: Taxi dance band at the Red Mill with Lavern Floyd
summary: His first weekly job was in a taxi dance hall where the band played one chorus per dime; the place burned down after seven or eight months.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well then, how did you get to get this job with Duke Ellighew?
Just from going down out in the

park and taking my horn and playing with all the little guys about the same age about twenty years old. And it actually was like a playground where they were playing. And finally they just, when a little job did show up, they knew that I was available and they called me to go to the Taxi dance. That was the first.....
That was the first sort of really .....
First weekly job I had.
Yes.
I'd been playing on gigs, a little bit here and a little bit there, but......
What would they be in those days, ten cents a dance or ...
That's what the girls made.
How long did you play for each dance?

One Chorus. One chorus, one thirty-two bar chorus. It was the beginning and the end of a song. So what we did was, we would go from one song right into another. Play one chorus of this. As soon as we switched songs, that's another dime for the house and for the girl.
Well now, what about the tempo? I mean if you played one chorus let's say of a slow ballad.......

Well sometimes we used to cheat and play half a chorus if it's slow and we always played, we always cut short on Saturday nights when the place would be filled with people and the shorter the better, the better it is for the guys.
Well I mean, you could quickly spend a dollar you know under those circumstances.

Yes. Well, see we played on at a place called "The Red Mill", dance hall and we were on North Main, way over by the court house, the Los Angeles Court House. in there at that time were mostly Filipinos. And they used to dress real sharp and look very nice. But they paid their money, they didn't care. ten cents for half a chorus. As long as we changed songs they knew that was the end of their dime.
Well did they, was the idea of those taxi dance halls to make assignments with the girls afterwards or anything like that?
Who, from the patrons you mean?
Yes.
No. But they did, but......
I man just having that quick dance with the girl presumably was not the height of their........
That was it for most of them.
Was it? The girls were not sort of prostitutes?
No, no. Not where we were. I guess maybe there is places like that where they kind of, you know, go into that business. But not, not at the club where I was.
You told me once that the, I think the leader of the band was a piano player, Lavern ....
Yes, Lavern yes, Lavern Floyd.
Yes, where did he come from? is still He was just out there?

Yes, He's still out there. Yes I got a, Benny Carter sent me a directory of the Los Angeles local and I just looked up some of these old guys to see if they were still there and they're still Lavern Floyd is still listed under
piano. Now he must be about 68 or 69 years old. He wasn't really too old.
Were there any other good musicians in this band or was it just a dance band?
It was just a dance band. It was mostly a dance band.
Well how long did you make it with them?

I stayed with them about seven or eight months. And the reason I left was the place caught fire. Yes, somebody left a lit cigarette in one of those big seats, and after the place was closed it caught fire. And it burned up everything. The drums, of course I had my trumpet, it didn't bother me.
But then we moved across the street into another building. But not for long. I didn't stay there too long, either, because Then I went to another band.
